<p>We then asked Europol to disclose the contents of those documents, or at least provide partial access, such as the titles of the documents. They refused to do so, citing protection of public interest and commercial interests. We appealed that decision and that appeal was denied. Europol was able to confirm, however, that they did not have access to other ad-based surveillance products produced by Babel Street and Rayzone.</p>



<p>At a <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EdTLOQGLUVI">conference</a> panel hosted by Computers, Privacy and Data Protection (CPDP) in May 2025 on the subject of “Advertisement Intelligence by European Agencies,” a senior data protection supervisor at Europol mentioned that his colleagues had presented him with a quote from a commercial intelligence provider based in Israel and asked his opinion if they could purchase it. He described the intelligence provider’s quote as saying “we will get you any information you need. So we will infiltrate, we will impersonate, we will hack into the system. Whatever it is you need, we will make sure you get it.” After studying the quote and the included terms and conditions, the data protection supervisor claimed that Europol’s data protection office stopped the procurement from going ahead. </p>



<h4 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Germany</strong></h4>



<p>A parliamentary inquiry asking the German federal government about whether it uses Webloc or other specific ad-based surveillance products was rejected, as reported by <a href="https://netzpolitik.org/2025/sicherheitsbehoerden-und-databroker-bundesregierung-macht-datenkauf-zum-staatsgeheimnis/">netzpolitik.org</a>. The inquiry excluded German intelligence agencies. The government refused to answer the parliament’s questions also for federal police forces citing national security reasons. The government however stated that the acquisition of personal data from data brokers can be appropriate in some cases.</p>



<h4 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Additional Research on European Countries</strong></h4>



<p>We found other information suggesting that Tangles, Webloc or other Cobwebs products are being sold in Europe countries: </p>



<ul class="wp-block-list">
<li><strong>Italy</strong>: The Local Police of Venice hosted a Tangles and Webloc <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20260331200330/https://www.linkedin.com/posts/sebianchi_team-training-projects-activity-6955629496179818496-7B9L/">training day</a> in July 2022, which suggests that Webloc has been in use in Italy at least for a brief time period. We are not aware of any information that clarifies whether Venice police conducted any assessment of the legal implications ahead of the event.  </li>
</ul>



<ul class="wp-block-list">
<li><strong>Netherlands</strong>: The Dutch company, DataExpert, is a reseller of Cobwebs products in Europe and specifically <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20260331200616/https://dataexpert.eu/products/osint-platforms-cobwebs-technologies/web-investigation-platform">advertises</a> Webloc capabilities claiming that “<em>Cobwebs lets you… use integrated ADINT (Advertisement Intelligence) functionalities</em>.” European public procurement <a href="https://ted.europa.eu/en/search/result?FT=dataexpert&search-scope=ALL&scope=ALL&onlyLatestVersions=false&sortColumn=publication-number&sortOrder=DESC&page=1&simpleSearchRef=true">records</a> show that DataExpert sold a number of software products in Europe between 2016 to 2026, including in Denmark, Belgium, and the Netherlands (the records do not state what product they sold to these governments). </li>
</ul>



<ul class="wp-block-list">
<li><strong>Germany</strong>: Cobwebs Technologies has a corporate entity registered in Germany since 2019. At some point, it was renamed from “Cobwebs GmbH” to “PEN-LINK GmbH.” Omri Timianker is listed as a director.<sup data-fn="1aad6b5a-92be-4e3f-96a1-178ee46259d4" class="fn"><a href="#1aad6b5a-92be-4e3f-96a1-178ee46259d4" id="1aad6b5a-92be-4e3f-96a1-178ee46259d4-link">34</a></sup> It has also been <a href="https://www.intelligenceonline.com/europe-russia/2022/11/11/bernhard-pawlak-brings-israeli-cyber-to-germany,109863868-art">reported</a> that Cobwebs had a sales representative based in Germany who was previously a sales representative at NSO Group.</li>
</ul>



<ul class="wp-block-list">
<li><strong>Spain</strong>: The Spanish company, Ondata International, is also a reseller of Cobwebs products. Procurement records <a href="https://ted.europa.eu/en/search/result?FT=ondata&search-scope=ALL&scope=ALL&onlyLatestVersions=false&sortColumn=publication-number&sortOrder=DESC&page=1">show</a> that they have sold a number of software products to Spain and Portugal in the last few years (the records do not suggest what product they sold).</li>
</ul>



<ul class="wp-block-list">
<li><strong>France</strong>: Cobwebs’ promotional materials, and subsequent reporting in the French press, <a href="https://www.brennancenter.org/sites/default/files/2021-09/Cobwebs%20Use%20Case.pdf;%20https://www.lequipe.fr/Football/Actualites/Un-dispositif-de-securite-exceptionnel-pour-la-finale-de-la-ligue-europa/901149">suggest</a> that the French police used Tangles to monitor audiences at the Atletico Madrid versus Marseille FC Europa League Final in 2018.</li>
</ul>



<p>Based on <a href="#6-Server-Infrastructure">technical analysis</a> detailed below, we identified active servers located in the Netherlands (32), Germany (8), France (2), Ireland (1), Sweden (1), Norway (1), and Cyprus (1) that we consider to be associated with Cobwebs product deployments. The Netherlands appear to be a major node in Cobwebs server infrastructure. One of the servers located in the Netherlands might be associated with a Webloc deployment, as detailed in <a href="#6-Server-Infrastructure"><strong>Section 6</strong></a><strong>.</strong> In our analysis, we found additional hosts which we consider to be associated with the wider Cobwebs server infrastructure located in Hungary, Poland, and Italy. We do not know whether the server locations represent customers located in these countries.</p>



<h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>United States</strong></h3>



<h4 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Department of Homeland Security</strong></h4>



<p>While ICE is a Webloc customer, as discussed in the previous section, other DHS components may have also purchased it. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) was a Tangles customer at least in 2024<sup data-fn="d9ce7575-2b31-4797-95c8-7eca77b3b317" class="fn"><a href="#d9ce7575-2b31-4797-95c8-7eca77b3b317" id="d9ce7575-2b31-4797-95c8-7eca77b3b317-link">35</a></sup> and it has utilized ad-based location data at least from 2019 to 2021, according to a <a href="https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/27714350-adid-efficacy-pilot-pta">document</a> released by the agency. The DHS also purchased annual Tangles licenses in <a href="https://www.usaspending.gov/award/CONT_AWD_70RDA124P00000009_7001_-NONE-_-NONE-">2024</a> and <a href="https://www.usaspending.gov/award/CONT_AWD_70RDA125P00000010_7001_-NONE-_-NONE-">2025</a> in “support” of its “insider threat program.” A <a href="https://sam.gov/opp/3073affc533f4741abc6e42f93957cb0/view">notice</a> related to the 2024 contract discusses “commercially available information” and “geo location data.” Monitoring “insider threats” <a href="https://crackedlabs.org/en/data-work/publications/securityriskprofiling">typically involves</a> monitoring an organization’s own employees. Another DHS component, the Office of Intelligence & Analysis (I&A), entered into a five-year <a href="https://media.unicornriot.ninja/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/cobwebs_and_tangles_redacted.pdf">Tangles contract</a> worth up to $3 million in 2020 and used the system to compile dossiers on protesters, according to an internal <a href="https://www.wyden.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/I&A%20and%20OGC%20Portland%20Reports.pdf">DHS report</a>. We consider CBP and the DHS’ insider threat program as potential Webloc customers.</p>



<h4 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Other Federal Customers</strong></h4>



<p>Additional federal Tangles customers in the U.S. include the <a href="https://www.usaspending.gov/award/CONT_AWD_140F1S23P0008_1448_-NONE-_-NONE-">Department of Justice (DOJ)</a>, the <a href="https://www.usaspending.gov/award/CONT_AWD_89303025FIG400032_8900_NNG15SD19B_8000">Department of Energy</a>, and the <a href="https://www.usaspending.gov/award/CONT_AWD_205AE922P00204_2050_-NONE-_-NONE-">Internal Revenue Service (IRS)</a>.</p>



<h4 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>State-Level Law Enforcement</strong> </h4>



<p>State-level law enforcement departments who purchased Tangles include the Vermont Department of Public Safety,<sup data-fn="86cb924e-ad5e-48c4-8ccd-1f5d9bc7cbee" class="fn"><a href="#86cb924e-ad5e-48c4-8ccd-1f5d9bc7cbee" id="86cb924e-ad5e-48c4-8ccd-1f5d9bc7cbee-link">36</a></sup> Illinois State Police,<sup data-fn="8aa57170-4121-434b-8fcc-fdab6541af17" class="fn"><a href="#8aa57170-4121-434b-8fcc-fdab6541af17" id="8aa57170-4121-434b-8fcc-fdab6541af17-link">37</a></sup> New York State Police,<sup data-fn="a28ef3d0-f08d-4495-bd18-41c75a574375" class="fn"><a href="#a28ef3d0-f08d-4495-bd18-41c75a574375" id="a28ef3d0-f08d-4495-bd18-41c75a574375-link">38</a></sup> Colorado Department of Public Safety,<sup data-fn="6f47a508-4d82-47d5-a387-67e1dba05f52" class="fn"><a href="#6f47a508-4d82-47d5-a387-67e1dba05f52" id="6f47a508-4d82-47d5-a387-67e1dba05f52-link">39</a></sup> Hawaii State Fusion Center,<sup data-fn="51fce29d-1c60-410b-950f-827e387b4bba" class="fn"><a href="#51fce29d-1c60-410b-950f-827e387b4bba" id="51fce29d-1c60-410b-950f-827e387b4bba-link">40</a></sup> and the <a href="https://washingtoncitypaper.com/article/753352/d-c-purchased-a-controversial-web-surveillance-platform-but-wont-say-how-theyre-using-it/">District of Columbia’s Homeland Security and Emergency Management Agency</a> (HSEMA). North Carolina’s State Bureau of Investigation (SBI) also used Cobwebs software.<sup data-fn="d8b16139-94cf-4229-9001-f213880b9321" class="fn"><a href="#d8b16139-94cf-4229-9001-f213880b9321" id="d8b16139-94cf-4229-9001-f213880b9321-link">41</a></sup> The Connecticut Judicial Marshall Services purchased “Threat Intelligence Software” from Cobwebs Technologies.<sup data-fn="74b76bb1-b6e4-4ac6-8e3a-bff6d0323538" class="fn"><a href="#74b76bb1-b6e4-4ac6-8e3a-bff6d0323538" id="74b76bb1-b6e4-4ac6-8e3a-bff6d0323538-link">42</a></sup> A <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20251003102043/https://www.jud.ct.gov/BidPortal/Docviewer/DocumentInquiry.aspx?DocID=133370&AppID=1">notice</a> related to the contract explained that Judicial Marshall Services aimed to use the system to monitor “potential civil unrest” and “subversive groups” in the context of threats against judges and employees.</p>



<h4 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Local Law Enforcement</strong></h4>



<p>A quote for a Tangles contract of San Joaquin Sheriff’s Office in California includes an option for “Webloc Geo source data,” according to <a href="https://www.eff.org/files/2025/08/18/pen-link_unredacted.pdf">documents</a> obtained via a freedom of information request, which was only made available after the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) <a href="https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2024/12/eff-goes-court-uncover-police-surveillance-tech-california">went to court</a>. While the Webloc option is not visible in the corresponding <a href="https://www.eff.org/files/2025/08/18/pen-link_unredacted.pdf">purchase order</a>, we still consider the sheriff’s office of San Joaquin a potential Webloc customer. We also consider the police department of Amarillo in Texas a potential Webloc customer, as it considered buying Tangles including the “ability to access, search and analyze mobile device communication records,” according to a <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20251003192513/https://www.amarillo.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Amarillo-City-Council-Agenda-Planner-September-3-2025.pdf">city council memo</a>. </p>



<p>As discussed in the previous section, the sheriff of Goliad County, also in Texas, discussed the use of Webloc in an interview while leaving it unclear whether his office had purchased the system by itself or accessed external resources. Several other police units in counties and cities in the U.S., both large and small, have purchased Tangles, including the police departments of Hartford,<sup data-fn="f1f93f64-cc1e-4b1b-8d3a-535e4e47f474" class="fn"><a href="#f1f93f64-cc1e-4b1b-8d3a-535e4e47f474" id="f1f93f64-cc1e-4b1b-8d3a-535e4e47f474-link">43</a></sup> <a href="https://www.texasobserver.org/texas-police-invest-tangles-sheriff-surveillance/">Houston</a>, Winston-Salem,<sup data-fn="65fcc67b-af21-47ec-aa89-39c48ad4417f" class="fn"><a href="#65fcc67b-af21-47ec-aa89-39c48ad4417f" id="65fcc67b-af21-47ec-aa89-39c48ad4417f-link">44</a></sup> <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20251027171623/https://www.pcbfl.gov/home/showpublisheddocument/23158/638271635414570000">Panama City Beach</a>, and <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20250413143423/https://www.princegeorgescountymd.gov/sites/default/files/media-document/dcv3930_current-contract-list-pdf.pdf">Prince George’s County</a> and the sheriff departments of <a href="https://cityclerk.lacity.org/onlinedocs/2023/23-0690_rpt_mayor_2-21-24.pdf">LA County</a>, Henry County,<sup data-fn="f58283da-9111-4f1f-834a-c1c2445ee027" class="fn"><a href="#f58283da-9111-4f1f-834a-c1c2445ee027" id="f58283da-9111-4f1f-834a-c1c2445ee027-link">45</a></sup> and Jackson County.<sup data-fn="0d5057e9-db96-45c5-ae62-25d698c75ec1" class="fn"><a href="#0d5057e9-db96-45c5-ae62-25d698c75ec1" id="0d5057e9-db96-45c5-ae62-25d698c75ec1-link">46</a></sup> A <em>Texas Observer</em> investigation <a href="https://www.texasobserver.org/texas-police-invest-tangles-sheriff-surveillance/">found</a> that “nearly 20 Texas sheriff’s offices have obtained a Tangles log-in.”</p>



<p>As information about such contracts is sparse and sometimes difficult or impossible to access, we assume that additional state and local agencies and departments other than the ones listed have purchased Tangles and Webloc.</p>



<h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Other Regions</strong></h3>



<h4 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Mexico</strong></h4>



<p>Several authorities in Mexico have acquired Tangles licenses through Karsos S.A. de C.V. including the <a href="https://www.asf.gob.mx/Trans/Informes/IR2022b/Documentos/Auditorias/2022_0835_a.pdf">Mexico State</a> prosecutor office, <a href="https://forbes.com.mx/la-policia-de-la-cdmx-tendra-un-simulador-de-tiro-en-realidad-virtual-de-73-mdp/">Mexico City</a>’s prosecutor office, and the <a href="https://www.excelsior.com.mx/nacional/ya-llego-a-mexico-iott-tangles-nuevo-ciberespionaje/1610932">State of Jalisco</a>. A media <a href="https://www.excelsior.com.mx/nacional/ya-llego-a-mexico-iott-tangles-nuevo-ciberespionaje/1610932">investigation</a> suggests that Webloc might have been included in one of the contracts in Mexico. In 2021, the Cobwebs <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20211217022028/https://cobwebs.com/contact-us/">website</a> listed an office in Mexico. Based on <a href="#6-Server-Infrastructure">technical analysis</a>, we identified two active servers located in Mexico that we consider to be associated with Cobwebs product deployments. As detailed in <a href="#6-Server-Infrastructure"><strong>Section 6</strong></a><strong>, </strong>one of the two servers might be associated with a Webloc deployment.</p>



<h4 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Colombia</strong></h4>



<p>Several documents confirm that Colombia’s public prosecutor office, Fiscalía General de la Nación (FGN) acquired licenses for Tangles. A <a href="https://blog.karisma.org.co/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/Cartilla_Cuando_el_estado_vigila_2_V_WEB-1.pdf">report</a> by the organization “Fundación Karisma” mentions a contract with “Desarrollo e Integración de Tecnología y Comunicaciones S.A.S. (Deinteko SAS)” with the purpose of “updating licence for Tangles platform.” Recent public financial <a href="https://www.fiscalia.gov.co/colombia/wp-content/uploads/Estados-financieros-a-2024-03-31-FGN.pdf">statements</a> of FGN confirm a new contract in 2024 with Deinteko for the “update and technical support of 8 Tangles licenses.” Based on <a href="#6-Server-Infrastructure">technical analysis</a>, we identified one active server located in Colombia that we consider to be associated with a Cobwebs product deployment.</p>



<h4 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Vietnam</strong></h4>



<p>Since at least 2024, a Vietnamese reseller has offered the Cobwebs products Tangles, Webloc, and Lynx on its <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20240526064745/https://asiccybersecurity.vn/san-pham/cobwebs-thu-thap-thong-tin/">website</a>. In addition, we discovered a Vietnamese Cobwebs-branded “Technical specifications” document dated 2021 on the web.<sup data-fn="c360e386-9a67-489d-b3b3-33b572093e9d" class="fn"><a href="#c360e386-9a67-489d-b3b3-33b572093e9d" id="c360e386-9a67-489d-b3b3-33b572093e9d-link">47</a></sup> The document appears to provide detailed contractual requirements for the deployment of a “WEBINT” system including the Cobwebs products Tangles, Lynx, Trapdoor and Webloc. The requirements listed in the document are very specific. For example, it states that the party implementing the Cobwebs system must have current deployments on Microsoft Azure Cloud in the Asia-Pacific region. The document might be related to a contract or it may represent merely a contractual template. The existence of a Vietnamese Webloc reseller, combined with a Vietnamese document that contains technical specifications for a Webloc deployment, raises the need for further research into potential Webloc customers in Vietnam. </p>



<h4 class="wp-block-heading">Singapore</h4>



<p>Cobwebs has had a corporate entity named “Cobwebs Asia Pte Ltd” <a href="https://opencorporates.com/companies/sg/201724268D">registered</a> in Singapore since 2017. The <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20260331150859/https://cwatechnologies.com/">website</a> of an entity named “CWA Webint Applications,” whose offerings match the descriptions of Tangles, Lynx and Trapdoor, shares the Singapore postal address displayed on the site with the registered address of Cobwebs Asia Pte Ltd. Based on <a href="#6-Server-Infrastructure">technical analysis</a>, we observed a server that we consider to be associated with a Cobwebs product deployment displaying a login page, whose design matches the design of Tangles login pages. We believe that CWA is either closely affiliated with or identical to Cobwebs. Overall, we identified 17 servers located in Singapore that we consider to be associated with the deployment of Cobwebs products. As detailed in <a href="#6-Server-Infrastructure"><strong>Section 6</strong></a>, two servers might be associated with Webloc and Trapdoor deployments. The current Penlink website <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20260331140935/https://www.penlink.com/contact-us/">offers</a> “Tangles Product Support” in Singapore.</p>



<h4 class="wp-block-heading">New Zealand</h4>



<p>In New Zealand, a 2022 report revealed that the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) had been using Cobwebs technology since 2019 to monitor all major platforms to “covertly collect people’s personal data.” The <a href="https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/476659/government-s-use-of-surveillance-firm-cobwebs-technologies-embroiled-in-controversy">report</a> states that it delivers this data to analysts in the MBIE Intelligence Unit, which is part of Immigration New Zealand. A later report in <a href="https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/524259/mbie-uses-fake-accounts-to-catch-immigration-fraudsters-and-migrant-exploiters">2024</a> by the same publication said that documents obtained by FOIs revealed that the intelligence unit had been questioned by watchdogs over their use of Cobwebs products and that the government admitted that “Cobwebs was bought to combat mass arrivals of asylumseekers [sic] by boat.” In 2024, an “automated register of false personas to use on social media platforms” was set up, according to documents obtained via a FOI request. This information <a href="https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/476659/government-s-use-of-surveillance-firm-cobwebs-technologies-embroiled-in-controversy">suggests</a> that the New Zealand government might have purchased not only Tangles, but also Lynx.</p>



<h4 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Israel</strong></h4>



<p>While Cobwebs Technologies has long been headquartered in <a href="#2-Cobwebs">Israel</a>, we are not aware of confirmed product deployments in the country. According to records on LinkedIn, three Israeli military personnel received Webloc training in 2022 and 2024 while working for the Israeli Defence Forces.<sup data-fn="b68f1940-96f7-4c8d-a8a6-44e313b5b737" class="fn"><a href="#b68f1940-96f7-4c8d-a8a6-44e313b5b737" id="b68f1940-96f7-4c8d-a8a6-44e313b5b737-link">48</a></sup> We <a href="#6-Server-Infrastructure">identified</a> 37 hosts located in Israel that we consider to be associated with the company’s server infrastructure.</p>



<h4 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Other Countries</strong></h4>



<p>We found information about the presence of Cobwebs products in additional countries. The 2021 version of the company’s website <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20211217022028/https://cobwebs.com/contact-us/">displayed</a> offices in Indonesia and India. The current PenLink website <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20260331140935/https://www.penlink.com/contact-us/">offers</a> “Tangles Product Support” in Thailand and Australia. Based on technical <a href="#6-Server-Infrastructure">analysis</a>, we identified active servers that we consider to be associated with Cobwebs product deployments located in Indonesia, Hong Kong, Japan, United Arab Emirates, Iraq, and Kenya. We identified an additional host in Brazil that we consider to be associated with Cobwebs Technologies’ server infrastructure.</p>



<h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Microsoft Offerings</strong></h3>



<p>While not a potential Webloc customer itself, Microsoft <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20220328225933/https://appsource.microsoft.com/en-us/product/web-apps/cobwebstechnologiesltd1604391859819.webloc">listed Webloc</a> as a “preferred solution” on its AppSource app store in 2022, which allowed customers to <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20220216222312/https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/marketplace/appsource-overview">find, try, buy, and deploy</a> the listed software. According to Microsoft, <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20220216222312/https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/marketplace/appsource-overview">preferred solutions</a> were “selected by a team of Microsoft experts” and come from “Microsoft partners with deep, proven expertise and capabilities to address specific customer needs.” Webloc was removed from the app store at some point after 2022. A <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20230207115908/https://cobwebs.com/press-releases/cobwebs-technologies-redefining-the-norms-of-cyber-intelligence/">press release</a> from Cobwebs Technologies published in 2019 suggests that “the company has been working with leading cloud providers, such as Microsoft” since at least 2019.</p>



<p>At the time of publication, Microsoft still lists several products developed by Cobwebs Technologies on its app store, now renamed <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20260320141229/https://marketplace.microsoft.com/en-us/">Microsoft Marketplace</a>, including <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20260320135229/https://marketplace.microsoft.com/en-us/product/cobwebstechnologiesltd1604391859819.tangles">Tangles</a>, <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20260320135241/https://marketplace.microsoft.com/en-us/product/saas/cobwebstechnologiesltd1604391859819.tangles_api">Tangles API</a>, <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20260320135414/https://marketplace.microsoft.com/en-us/product/cobwebstechnologiesltd1604391859819.lynx">Lynx</a>, <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20260320135427/https://marketplace.microsoft.com/en-us/product/cobwebstechnologiesltd1604391859819.weaver">Weaver</a>, and <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20260320135650/https://marketplace.microsoft.com/en-us/product/cobwebstechnologiesltd1604391859819.threat_intelligence">Threat Intelligence Solution</a>. Technical <a href="#6-Server-Infrastructure">analysis</a> suggests that 219 out of the 298 active hosts affiliated with Cobwebs Technologies’ server infrastructure are hosted in data centers related to Microsoft’s Azure cloud.</p>



<h2 class="wp-block-heading" id="6-Server-Infrastructure"><strong>6. Cobwebs Server Infrastructure</strong></h2>



<p>After receiving a tip about Cobweb’s infrastructure from colleagues at Amnesty International’s <a href="https://securitylab.amnesty.org/">Security Lab</a>, we mapped out server infrastructure that we consider to be associated with deployments of Cobwebs products on servers located in at least 21 countries. We do not know whether the server locations represent customers located in these countries.</p>



<p>Our technical analysis identifies domains, subdomains, and other web hosts that we consider to be associated with Cobwebs Technologies using common DNS telemetry and IP geolocation tools, the URL telemetry tool Censys, and browser testing. We accessed only publicly available resources without any modification or circumvention of access controls.</p>



<h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Cobwebs Domains and Login Pages</strong></h3>



<p>First, we identified three domains affiliated with Cobwebs’ server infrastructure.</p>



<p>The domain cobwebsapp.com is linked to a SSL certificate registered by Cobwebs Technologies using the address of its Israeli corporate entity.<sup data-fn="82cd3f15-031d-4d0e-890e-72fbbb4d4665" class="fn"><a href="#82cd3f15-031d-4d0e-890e-72fbbb4d4665" id="82cd3f15-031d-4d0e-890e-72fbbb4d4665-link">49</a></sup> The domains cwtapp.com and cwsystem.com are not directly linked to an entity. Common DNS telemetry tools observed 520 subdomains for these three domains, 284 of them resolving to particular IP addresses as of January 30, 2026.</p>



<p>When we viewed the active subdomains in the web browser, 81 of the cwtapp.com subdomains and 35 of the cwsystem.com subdomains displayed a login page containing a Tangles logo, as of March 6, 2026.</p>

<h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Tangles Servers</strong></h3>



<p>Combining browser testing with an analysis of subdomain naming schemes, we conclude that 205 out of 284  currently resolving subdomains for cobwebsapp.com, cwtapp.com, and cwsystem.com may represent Tangles servers.</p>



<figure class="wp-block-table alignwide"><table><thead><tr><th><strong>Domain</strong></th><th><strong>Subdomains with particular naming</strong></th><th><strong>Examples</strong></th><th><strong>Subdomains currently resolving</strong></th><th><strong>Subdomains with Tangles login page</strong></th><th><strong>Conclusion</strong></th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td><strong>cobwebsapp.com</strong></td><td>85 subdomain names contain the letters ‘tg’ and a number or acronym</td><td>s703-tg.cobwebsapp.com<br>tg-173.cobwebsapp.com<br>tg-zu.cobwebsapp.com</td><td>58</td><td>0</td><td>58 cobwebsapp.com subdomains may represent Tangles servers</td></tr><tr><td><strong>cwtapp.com</strong></td><td>126 subdomain names contain the letters ‘tg’ and a number<br><br>23 subdomain names contain the letter ‘s’ and a number</td><td>s255-tg.cwtapp.com<br><br><br><br>s1688.cwtapp.com</td><td>81<br><br><br><br>18</td><td>66<br><br><br><br>15</td><td>Up to 99 cwtapp.com subdomains may represent Tangles servers</td></tr><tr><td><strong>cwsystem.com</strong></td><td>62 subdomain names contain the letters ‘tg’ and a number<br><br>32 subdomain names contain the letter ‘p’ and a number</td><td>p83-tg.cwsystem.com<br><br><br><br>p07.cwsystem.com<br>p156.cwsystem.com</td><td>31<br><br><br><br>17</td><td>15<br><br><br><br>10</td><td>Up to 48 cwsystem.com subdomains may represent Tangles servers</td></tr><tr><td></td><td></td><td></td><td></td><td></td><td><strong>Up to 205 potential Tangles servers</strong></td></tr></tbody></table><figcaption class="wp-element-caption"><strong>Table 5</strong><br>Analysis of potential Tangles servers</figcaption></figure>



<p style="margin-top:var(--wp--preset--spacing--70)">As <strong>Table 5</strong> shows, a significant number of subdomain names that contain the letters ‘tg’, ‘s’ or ‘p’, combined with a number or acronym, display a Tangles login page when accessing it in the web browser. We thus consider all subdomains following this naming scheme as potential Tangles servers. </p>



<p>While we were not able to access any cobwebsapp.com subdomain in the web browser, the naming scheme is very similar to the naming scheme observed for many cwtapp.com subdomains. A <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20260331181021/https://media.unicornriot.ninja/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/cobwebs_and_tangles_redacted.pdf">licensing document</a> related to a contract covering Tangles and Lynx by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) from the year 2021, obtained via a freedom of information request, confirms the assumption that subdomains containing the letters ‘tg’ refer to deployments of Tangles. It also indicates that a subdomain containing the letters ‘um’ refers to Cobwebs’ user management system, which appears to allow a Cobwebs customer to determine who gets access to a system.</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-full"><img decoding="async" width="793" height="680" src="data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAxkAAAKoAQMAAAAhzKDYAAAAA1BMVEVHcEyC+tLSAAAAAXRSTlMAQObYZgAAAFlJREFUeNrtwTEBAAAAwqD1T20Gf6AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAADgNwxXAAHQiOptAAAAAElFTkSuQmCC" alt="" class="wp-image-88858 lazyload" title="Figure 12"   data-src="https://citizenlab.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/image-6.png" data-srcset="https://citizenlab.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/image-6.png 793w, https://citizenlab.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/image-6-300x257.png 300w, https://citizenlab.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/image-6-768x659.png 768w" data-sizes="auto" data-eio-rwidth="793" data-eio-rheight="680" /><noscript><img decoding="async" width="793" height="680" src="https://citizenlab.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/image-6.png" alt="" class="wp-image-88858" title="Figure 12" srcset="https://citizenlab.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/image-6.png 793w, https://citizenlab.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/image-6-300x257.png 300w, https://citizenlab.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/image-6-768x659.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 793px) 100vw, 793px" data-eio="l" /></noscript><div class="wp-block-image__meta"><div class="wp-block-image__title">Figure 12</div><figcaption class="wp-element-caption">Licensing document related to a DHS contract</figcaption></div></figure>



<p>We have high confidence in the assessment that subdomains that displayed Tangles login pages are associated with Tangles product deployments. We have medium confidence in the assessment that subdomains that did not display a login page but are following a similar naming scheme are associated with Cobwebs product deployments.</p>



<h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Servers Related to Other Products</strong></h3>



<p>A few subdomains appear to refer to other Cobwebs products, 10 of them resolving to particular IP addresses as of January 30, 2026. Subdomains containing the letters ‘td’ may refer to Trapdoor, subdomains containing the letters ‘wr’ may refer to Weaver, and subdomains containing the letters ‘wl’ may refer to Webloc. Subdomains containing the letters ‘um’ may refer to Cobwebs user management system, as discussed above.</p>



<figure class="wp-block-table"><table><thead><tr><th><strong>Domain</strong></th><th><strong>Subdomain naming scheme</strong></th><th><strong>Example subdomains</strong></th><th><strong>Interpretation</strong></th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td rowspan="4"><strong>cobwebsapp.com</strong></td><td>14 subdomain names contain the letters ‘um’</td><td>s637-um.cobwebsapp.com</td><td rowspan="4">29 cobwebsapp.com subdomains may refer to servers related to Trapdoor, Weaver, Webloc and Cobwebs’ user management system, 8 of them currently resolving</td></tr><tr><td>6 subdomain names contain the letters ‘td’</td><td>s470-td.cobwebsapp.com</td></tr><tr><td>4 subdomain names contain the letters ‘wr’</td><td>wr-s361.cobwebsapp.com</td></tr><tr><td>5 subdomain names contain the letters ‘wl’</td><td>s704-wl.cobwebsapp.com</td></tr><tr><td><strong>cwtapp.com</strong></td><td>1 subdomain name contains the letters ‘um’</td><td>s725-um.cwtapp.com</td><td>1 cwtapp.com subdomain may refer to a server related to Cobwebs’ user management system, currently not resolving</td></tr><tr><td rowspan="2"><strong>cwsystem.com</strong></td><td>2 subdomain contain the letters ‘um’</td><td>p03-um.cwsystem.com</td><td rowspan="2">3 cwsystem.com subdomains refer to servers related to Trapdoor and Cobwebs’ user management system, 2 of them still resolving</td></tr><tr><td>1 subdomain contains the letters ‘td’</td><td>s883-td.cwsystem.com</td></tr></tbody></table><figcaption class="wp-element-caption"><strong>Table 6</strong><br>Potential servers related to Trapdoor, Weaver, Webloc and Cobwebs’ user management system</figcaption></figure>



<p>We have medium confidence in the assessment that subdomains containing the letters ‘td’, ‘wr’, and ‘wl’ refer to servers associated with deployments of the Cobwebs products Trapdoor, Weaver, and Webloc.</p>



<h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>More Cobwebs Servers and Login Pages</strong></h3>



<p>We identified 14 additional servers associated with Cobwebs based on searching for hosts associated with certificates linked to the Cobwebs domains cobwebsapp.com and cwtapp.com with the URL telemetry tool Censys. Most of the 14 hosts were running a web server listening to particular ports, as of 30 January, 2026. When accessing those hosts in a web browser, four of them displayed login pages including logos for Trapdoor, Weaver, and Cobwebs’ user management system. Some of the login masks appeared to be broken (see below screenshots for examples). Another host displayed an error page containing multiple references to Tangles.</p>

<h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Cobwebs Server Geolocations</strong></h3>



<p>Based on the above research, we identified 219 active servers we assess as associated with Cobwebs product deployments. With the help of common IP geolocation tools we then retrieved the likely server locations of the corresponding IP addresses.</p>



<p>As a result, we found that many potential Cobwebs product servers are located in the U.S. (126), Netherlands (32), Singapore (17), Germany (8), Hong Kong (8), and the U.K. (7). We also identified potential product servers located in Kenya, Iraq, United Arab Emirates, Indonesia, India, Mexico, Colombia, Australia, Japan, and in several European countries (France, Sweden, Norway, Ireland, and Cyprus). We found only one potential product server located in Cobwebs Technologies’ home country, Israel.</p>



<figure class="wp-block-table"><table><thead><tr><th><strong>Country</strong></th><th><strong>Potential product servers</strong></th><th><strong>All servers</strong></th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>U.S.</td><td>126</td><td>127</td></tr><tr><td>Germany</td><td>8</td><td>38</td></tr><tr><td>Israel</td><td>1</td><td>37</td></tr><tr><td>Netherlands</td><td>32</td><td>33</td></tr><tr><td>Singapore</td><td>17</td><td>17</td></tr><tr><td>Hong Kong</td><td>8</td><td>10</td></tr><tr><td>U.K.</td><td>7</td><td>7</td></tr><tr><td>Japan</td><td>2</td><td>3</td></tr><tr><td>Australia</td><td>3</td><td>3</td></tr><tr><td>Sweden</td><td>1</td><td>2</td></tr><tr><td>Mexico</td><td>2</td><td>2</td></tr><tr><td>Italy</td><td></td><td>2</td></tr><tr><td>India</td><td>1</td><td>2</td></tr><tr><td>Indonesia</td><td>1</td><td>2</td></tr><tr><td>France</td><td>2</td><td>2</td></tr><tr><td>U.A.E.</td><td>2</td><td>2</td></tr><tr><td>Poland</td><td></td><td>1</td></tr><tr><td>Norway</td><td>1</td><td>1</td></tr><tr><td>Kenya</td><td>1</td><td>1</td></tr><tr><td>Iraq</td><td>1</td><td>1</td></tr><tr><td>Ireland</td><td>1</td><td>1</td></tr><tr><td>Hungary</td><td></td><td>1</td></tr><tr><td>Cyprus</td><td>1</td><td>1</td></tr><tr><td>Colombia</td><td>1</td><td>1</td></tr><tr><td>Brazil</td><td></td><td>1</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Total</strong></td><td><strong>219</strong></td><td><strong>298</strong></td></tr></tbody></table><figcaption class="wp-element-caption"><strong>Table 7</strong><br>Servers potentially associated with Cobwebs product deployments and its wider server infrastructure.</figcaption></figure>



<p>When considering all hosts including those we cannot attribute to product deployments, we identified 298 servers associated with Cobwebs server infrastructure located in 25 countries. This includes all currently resolving cobwebsapp.com, cwtapp.com, and cwsystem.com subdomains and the additional hosts identified via Censys. According to this analysis, we identified servers in additional countries (Brazil, Italy, Poland, Hungary) and a much higher number of servers located in Israel (37). Notably, 71 servers are located in the Netherlands and Germany. Most of the U.S. servers are located in the state of Virginia, followed by Washington, California, Arizona, Texas, Illinois, and Oregon.</p>



<p>According to an analysis of IP addresses, 219 out of the 298 active hosts affiliated with Cobwebs Technologies’ server infrastructure are hosted in data centres related to Microsoft’s Azure cloud.</p>



<p>Some host names associated with Cobwebs product servers have been resolving to the same IP address for only a few months. Many have been active for several years. IP addresses of product servers that have been active only in the past are currently located in additional countries (Switzerland, Portugal, and Lithuania).</p>



<p>While we have high confidence in the list of countries where we identified active servers associated with Cobwebs products, we know neither whether these products are actually in operation, nor whether the customers who are potentially using Tangles and other Cobwebs products are located in the same countries as the located servers. We do not consider our map of Cobwebs product servers to be exhaustive. While we identified 219 potential product servers, the numbering in the subdomain names ranges from low digits up to 1704.</p>

<p>Cobwebs Technologies has links to the spyware vendor Quadream through Cobweb Technologies’ founder Omri Timianker and investor Uri Ashkenazi. The Citizen Lab previously <a href="https://citizenlab.ca/research/spyware-vendor-quadream-exploits-victims-customers/">revealed</a> that Quadream’s spyware was used to target civil society in North America, Central Asia, Southeast Asia, Europe, and the Middle East. Victims included journalists and political opposition figures. While it was <a href="https://www.intelligenceonline.com/americas/2023/09/05/palm-beach-networks-eyes-quadream-s-technology,110039529-art">reported</a> that Quadream was trying to sell its assets in 2023, it is unclear whether it has managed to do so, and, according to company registration documents, Quadream continues to operate as an entity in Israel. According to company registration documents from Israel, both Timianker and Ashkenazi are also affiliated with a company called I-OTT, an intelligence and surveillance technology firm that has <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20170715222734/http://www.i-ott.com/index.php/en/solutions/covert-operations">advertised</a> providing “combat training” for “guerrilla warfare” and consultations on “covert operations.”</p>



<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Cobwebs Founder: Omri Timianker </h3>



<p>Omri Timianker is the founder of Cobwebs Technologies Ltd. and now oversees Penlink’s international operations.<sup data-fn="0e56ece4-3736-441f-84b6-89c31e0196c0" class="fn"><a href="#0e56ece4-3736-441f-84b6-89c31e0196c0" id="0e56ece4-3736-441f-84b6-89c31e0196c0-link">51</a></sup> According to documents obtained from Israel’s company register, he also has an indirect interest in Quadream Ltd. <strong>Figure 14</strong> contains information obtained from the Israel’s company register and reveals the ownership chain that links Timianker with Quadream.</p>



<p>Timianker’s LinkedIn profile<sup data-fn="2d1e4ee9-0cbb-48d6-9cec-1c5bcd57c9b4" class="fn"><a href="#2d1e4ee9-0cbb-48d6-9cec-1c5bcd57c9b4" id="2d1e4ee9-0cbb-48d6-9cec-1c5bcd57c9b4-link">52</a></sup> claims that as co-founder and president of Cobwebs (2015-2024), his key achievements included “scaling global operations across government and commercial markets” and “driving hundreds of large-scale deployments in complex environments.” According to his LinkedIn, he is now “General Manager International” at Penlink and responsible for leading “global growth and market expansion for Penlink across all regions outside the Americas.” </p>



<p>In 2025, Timianker co-founded insAIghts Academy, a digital intelligence “academy” with training hubs in Israel, London and the U.S.<sup data-fn="d705e144-561e-45f2-b2fb-527e046b1a4b" class="fn"><a href="#d705e144-561e-45f2-b2fb-527e046b1a4b" id="d705e144-561e-45f2-b2fb-527e046b1a4b-link">53</a></sup> A promotional video on <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BheuyC77kpc">YouTube</a> for the training centre in London states that the “purpose of insAIghts is to train the intelligence officers of the future.” InsAIghts offers training on “deep data extraction” enabling participants to “gain the ability to uncover essential, hidden information.” InsAIghts offers their <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20260331202459/https://www.penlink.com/insaights-academy-english/">training</a> not only to law enforcement but also to those who work in finance or the “corporate world.” </p>



<p>According to the firm’s website, Timianker is also on the advisory <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20260331202556/https://titan-ventures.com/">board</a> of Titan Ventures, a venture capital firm that invests in Israel’s cyber-intelligence sector. It <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20260331202556/https://titan-ventures.com/">claims</a> that it has gained “deep market understanding and expertise through years of involvement,” and is able to “identify the lack of adequate intelligence solutions to cope with the current technological and operational challenges.” According to his LinkedIn <a href="https://www.linkedin.com/in/omri-timianker-2a41925/">profile</a>, Timianker also co-founded I-OTT (2011-2021). Timianker, according to his <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20260331202556/https://titan-ventures.com/">bio</a> on the Titan Ventures website, also founded I-OTT (see below). </p>



<h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Uri Ashkenazi </strong></h3>



<p>As previously reported by the Citizen Lab, Uri Ashkenazi is an Israeli <a href="https://www.intelligenceonline.com/middle-east-and-africa/2022/07/28/ori-ashkenazi-builds-up-his-interests-in-israeli-cyber-intelligence,109802586-art">financier</a> who invests in Israel’s cyber intelligence sector, primarily through his venture capital firm, Titan Ventures. Ashkenazi has been a key investor in Quadream, Cobwebs, Falkor, and I-OTT. <em>Intelligence Online</em> <a href="https://www.intelligenceonline.com/middle-east-and-africa/2022/04/21/pcs-increasingly-essential-to-israeli-cyber-specialists-in-the-city-state,109779575-eve">reported</a> that he also previously served as a senior vice president of finance at Cobwebs. According to his LinkedIn <a href="https://www.linkedin.com/in/ori-ashkenazi-6aa19221/details/experience/">profile</a> he served in this role from January 2017 to October 2018. </p>



<p>Ashkenazi is closely connected to Omri Timianker. When Timianker posted news of the Penlink partnership on LinkedIn, Ashkenazi responded that it had been an “honor and privilege to invest, partner and support you guys from the early days.” To which Timianker replied “Thanks Ori Ashkenazi my Trustable friend, lets continue to rock and rolltogether.<em>”</em><sup data-fn="fb481a10-8dee-4dc3-9472-3b34fac9ec01" class="fn"><a href="#fb481a10-8dee-4dc3-9472-3b34fac9ec01" id="fb481a10-8dee-4dc3-9472-3b34fac9ec01-link">54</a></sup> In addition to the pair being connected through Cobwebs, Ashkenazi and Timianker are linked through I-OTT, Titan Ventures, and D&Y Ventures; Ashkenazi is the managing <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20260331202556/https://titan-ventures.com/">partner</a> of Titan Ventures and according to Israel corporate records, also a shareholder in D&Y Ventures and a shareholder in I-OTT. </p>



<h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>I-OTT</strong></h3>



<p>On its <a href="https://www.i-ott.com/">website</a>, I-OTT  advertises itself as “customized intelligence solutions for governmental and private agencies” and claims to have offices in Israel, Mexico and Brazil. According to the website, Cobwebs and Titan Ventures are part of the I-OTT “family.” </p>



<p>The 2017 version of its website reveals I-OTT product capabilities claiming that their “analysts have a rich military and civilian intelligence background, powerful automated WEBINT systems and the support of virtual persona (sock puppet),” and that they could provide “targeted research reports concerning almost any topic” including “social unrest.” They also <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20170716201952/http://www.i-ott.com/index.php/en/services/analysts-center">claim</a> to be operating “tailor-made avatars for collecting sensitive information.” In addition to their technology offering, I-OTT <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20170717153256/http://www.i-ott.com/index.php/en/services/operational-training2">offered</a> “advanced combat training” and claimed to “provide the basic effective ‘toolbox’ for anti-terror and guerrilla warfare,” <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20170715222734/http://www.i-ott.com/index.php/en/solutions/covert-operations">along</a> with “training and consulting about covert operations and units.”</p>



<p>According to <em>Intelligence Online</em>, the company Falkor is a spin off of I-OTT and <a href="https://www.intelligenceonline.com/gazette/2025/02/27/amos-malka-joins-falkor-sahar-in-singapour-egyptian-maritime-surveillance,110380543-art">specializes</a> in mass data analysis. Falkor’s website <a href="https://falkor.ai/products/">urges</a> its customers through the use of their products to “connect to OSINT and SOCMINT sources and enrich your data with new identifiers, associated online accounts, posts, and more. Conduct digital profiling and monitor topics of interest in real-time.”</p>



<h2 class="wp-block-heading" id="8-Trapdoor"><strong>8. Trapdoor</strong></h2>



<p>We present additional research on Trapdoor, a product developed by Cobwebs Technologies that has rarely been discussed publicly. In a 2020 article, the trade press site <em>Intelligence Online</em> <a href="https://www.intelligenceonline.com/surveillance--interception/2020/05/27/covid-19-pandemic-brings-cobwebs-into-the-light,108407395-art">reported</a> that Trapdoor is a Cobwebs solution “reserved for government customers.” We do not know whether Trapdoor is still being sold by Penlink. In its response to the Citizen Lab, Penlink <a href="https://citizenlab.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Citizen-Lab-Mail-Fwd_-Citizen-Lab-research-report_Redacted.pdf" rel="nofollow">claims</a>, without being specific, that our report describes “products that no longer exist.”</p>



<h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Cobwebs Website</strong></h3>



<p>The 2021 website of Cobwebs Technologies promoted Trapdoor as a system for “active web intelligence” that allows customers to “[a]nonymously engage with threat actors with various communication methods” and “re-build any link from across the web” in order to “gather intelligence” from devices including IP addresses, device type, “cookies,” and language settings. Trapdoor would <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20210513075343/https://cobwebs.com/products/active-web-intelligence/">facilitate</a> the “remote extraction of technical details with non-intrusive methods,” but also provides “methods to launch directed command modules at a connected source.” These promotional phrases are rather hard to parse.</p>



<h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Trapdoor Specifications</strong></h3>



<p>A Vietnamese “Technical Specifications” document<sup data-fn="bb64506b-d1da-4cf2-8ddf-551f2f36c741" class="fn"><a href="#bb64506b-d1da-4cf2-8ddf-551f2f36c741" id="bb64506b-d1da-4cf2-8ddf-551f2f36c741-link">55</a></sup> dated 2021 and branded “Cobwebs Technologies” we discovered publicly available on the web contains a clearer description of Trapdoor capabilities. The document appears to provide contractual requirements for the deployment of a “WEBINT” system including the Cobwebs products Tangles, Lynx, Trapdoor, and Webloc. The requirements listed in the document are very specific, overlapping with product descriptions from other sources in several ways.</p>



<p>While the document is largely in Vietnamese, the Trapdoor requirements section refers to the system as “SEP/Trapdoor” in English. The Vietnamese term used in the section translates to “social engineering platform.” We conclude that the document describes Trapdoor as a “social engineering platform,” in short “SEP.”</p>



<p>The Trapdoor section describes requirements the system must meet and thus makes suggestions about the system’s capabilities. As translated by the authors of this report with the help of machine translation tools, it states that:</p>



<ul class="wp-block-list">
<li>Trapdoor is a “web-based social engineering module to actively interact with targets,” separate from the “passive intelligence systems” for “web intelligence” and “avatar management” from the same vendor.</li>



<li>The system provides the ability to “generate phishing links disguised as any web link that can be sent to targets” via email or SMS. It supports “link obfuscation” using “URL shorteners,” supporting the “redirection of visitors to specified websites without exposing server details.” It allows “analysts to apply social engineering techniques such as sending pop-ups, pages, and input requests” to collect information.</li>



<li>It includes tools to “rapidly design full web pages or pop-ups deployed on the target side,” supporting “styling, content editing, image modification, input requests, file attachments, mobile and desktop compatibility.” It supports “URLs across multiple domains” that can be “registered anonymously, with flexibility for the end user to choose domain names.”</li>



<li>It maintains a “list of all links or websites accessed through the system.” It “route[s] and “host[s] target connections through proxy infrastructure and ensure anonymity and non-traceability,” provides a “dashboard” showing “real-time and historical connection data” and triggers “alerts” upon “target connection.”</li>



<li>It “automatically extract[s] available information from target connections” including IP address, browser type, language, version and plugins, operating system and version, device type, CPU and GPU information, screen resolution, ISP information, estimated geolocation, user inputs, timezone, battery level and charging status. If available it also provides “social media details” and “location network details.”</li>



<li>The system includes a “keylogger to record keystrokes, including potential capture of usernames and passwords.”</li>



<li>In addition, it allows “analysts to perform actions on the target’s browser, including terminating active connections, opening hidden tabs, extracting media from the target device, sending pop-ups, and delivering files or payloads.”</li>
</ul>



<h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Trapdoor Source Code</strong></h3>

Based on our analysis, we assess that the code represents a version of the Javascript source code of the Trapdoor admin interface used by customers to operate the system.</p>

<h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Analysis and Assessment of Trapdoor Capabilities</strong></h3>



<p>The descriptions of Trapdoor capabilities on the 2021 Cobwebs website and in the Vietnamese “Technical Specifications” document, in combination with the source code analysis, suggest that Trapdoor helps customers to trick victims into revealing information by sending them phishing links that lead to fake web pages, which are also created with the help of Trapdoor.</p>



<p>When a victim accesses those fake web pages, the system provides the Trapdoor customer with information entered by the victim, which can include keystrokes, usernames and passwords, and with information on the victim’s device. Most device attributes that can be extracted from “target connections” according to the Vietnamese document, are clearly accessible to website operators without compromising the victim’s device, including IP, device and browser information. Battery level and charging status of a device have also been <a href="https://lukaszolejnik.com/AssessingPrivacyWebStandardsIWPE17.pdf">accessible</a> to parties who serve web pages to someone’s browser.</p>



<p>In addition, our analysis suggests that Trapdoor customers can remotely carry out offensive actions that affect the victim’s browser or device. This includes opening pop-up windows and hidden tabs in the victim’s web browser and even “delivering files or payloads” to the victim’s device. According to the commonly used <a href="https://www.cloudflare.com/en-gb/learning/security/glossary/malicious-payload/">definition</a> in the cybersecurity context, the term “payload” typically refers to malicious software downloaded to a device. Based on our analysis, we assess that Trapdoor can help facilitate the deployment of malware on a victim’s device but does not include remote device infection or malware capabilities itself.</p>



<p>Our analysis of the technical specifications and the source code also leads us to conclude that Trapdoor can likely provide at least some capabilities typically provided by malware compromising a device’s operating system, including access to “media from the target device,”<sup data-fn="94142bbb-715e-4275-a015-0e65e830d892" class="fn"><a href="#94142bbb-715e-4275-a015-0e65e830d892" id="94142bbb-715e-4275-a015-0e65e830d892-link">56</a></sup> camera and microphone. As the system focuses on the extraction of information based on web pages visited by the victim, we assume that access to camera and microphone is or was also based on code executed in the victim’s web browser.</p>



<p>As discussed above, Cobwebs Technologies’ 2021 website <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20210513075343/https://cobwebs.com/products/active-web-intelligence/">referred to</a> Trapdoor as a system for “active web intelligence” that facilitates “remote extraction of technical details with non-intrusive methods” but also provides “methods to launch directed command modules at a connected source.”</p>



<p>Our findings on Trapdoor capabilities align with the findings in the “<a href="https://about.fb.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/Threat-Report-on-the-Surveillance-for-Hire-Industry.pdf">Threat Report on the Surveillance-for-Hire Industry</a>” published by Meta in 2021, which observed that “accounts used by Cobwebs customers also engaged in social engineering to join closed communities and forums and trick people into revealing personal information.” While Cobwebs Technologies <a href="https://en.globes.co.il/en/article-spire-capital-buys-israeli-web-intelligence-co-cobwebs-1001452029">stated</a> that the report was “false,” the research laid out in this section suggests that Meta had observed an application of  Trapdoor’s capabilities in the wild.</p>

<h2 class="wp-block-heading" id="9-responses"><strong>9. Response</strong> from Penlink</h2>



<p>On April 3, 2026, we sent a <a href="https://citizenlab.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Citizen-Lab_Penlink-2026.pdf" rel="nofollow">summary</a> of our findings to Penlink and offered them the opportunity to reply, which we publish <a href="https://citizenlab.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Citizen-Lab-Mail-Fwd_-Citizen-Lab-research-report_Redacted.pdf" rel="nofollow">here</a> in full.</p>



<p>Penlink claims in its response to the Citizen Lab that our findings “appear to rely on either inaccurate information or a misunderstanding about how we operate, including practices that Penlink does not engage in following our acquisition of Cobwebs Technologies in 2023.” It states that we “identify companies and products that no longer exist,” as well as “list countries we do not do business in” or “describe products incorrectly,” without being specific about the companies, products and countries. The response further states that “Penlink complies with U.S. state privacy laws” and that “Penlink understands the sensitivity and complexity of data privacy and operates under thoughtful compliance, due diligence, and responsible-use standards.” </p>



<p>We address some issues raised by Penlink in several places throughout the report. Its response leaves many of the questions we sent to them unanswered, adding to the lack of information it publicly provides about Webloc, its capabilities, customers, and uses. The response also does not address compliance with privacy and data protection laws outside the U.S., including in Europe.</p>



<h2 class="wp-block-heading" id="10-Conclusion"><strong>10. Conclusion</strong></h2>



<p>Both Cobwebs Technologies, which developed Webloc, and its successor Penlink, which has been selling Webloc since 2023, do not provide much public information about the system and its customers. This report provides a first comprehensive mapping of the capabilities, data processing practices, and customers of Webloc, a mass surveillance system that relies on data purchased from everyday consumer apps and digital advertising that provides information on the whereabouts, movements and personal characteristics of entire populations.</p>



<h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Intrusive Mass Surveillance</strong></h3>



<p>Webloc monitors hundreds of millions of people globally based on commercial data obtained from smartphones and other mobile devices they use. Even if a customer uses Webloc to track only a few individuals, the system still processes a constantly updated data stream on a large number of people without probable cause. </p>



<p>Location data and similar data collected from apps and digital advertising are highly sensitive. They can <a href="https://crackedlabs.org/en/rtb-security-crisis">reveal</a> information about a person’s home, workplace, family, friends, religion, political views, sexual orientation or health issues. Even if locations that are considered sensitive were removed from the data, it can still reveal information about a person’s home, workplace, family, friends, habits, and interests. As such, we consider Webloc to be an intrusive mass surveillance system.</p>



<h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Disproportionate Surveillance</strong></h3>



<p>In his <a href="https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/706321/means-of-control-by-byron-tau/">book</a> on the origins of ad-based surveillance in the U.S., investigative journalist Byron Tau shows how these technologies, initially built for U.S. military and intelligence operations in war zones, were eventually also deployed domestically by federal law enforcement agencies and then trickled down to state and local police. A local police department in the U.S., which purchased Webloc for border security and sex trafficking investigations, explained that it soon discovered other applications of the technology and began to use the system for routine criminal cases with damages of a few thousand dollars, according to an internal report discussed in <a href="#4-Customers"><strong>Section 4</strong></a>. This type of mission creep is particularly concerning because of the disproportionate nature of ad-based surveillance systems and because our findings show such systems are now used by military, intelligence and law enforcement agencies, including local police units, in several countries around the globe.</p>



<h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Legally Questionable</strong></h3>



<p>The systematic misuse of data purchased from everyday consumer apps and digital advertising for warrantless surveillance raises serious concerns about <a href="https://cdt.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/2021-12-08-Legal-Loopholes-and-Data-for-Dollars-Report-final.pdf">civil liberties</a> and <a href="https://www.interface-eu.org/publications/disproportionate-use-commercially-and-publicly-available-data-europes-next-frontier">fundamental rights</a>, particularly when used to target vulnerable groups such as immigrants or those who exercise their freedom of expression and assembly rights. Ad-based surveillance raises specific concerns when applied by organizations or governments, which are prone to authoritarianism or have weak or limited oversight. It generally raises concerns when governments lack a lawful basis to use it or when the underlying data is processed without a lawful basis.</p>



<p>In the U.S. and in Europe, both the lawfulness of governments using ad-based data for surveillance and the lawfulness of sharing the data over the entire supply chain, from apps and advertising firms to data brokers and surveillance vendors, are highly controversial.</p>



<p>In recent cases against several data brokers in the U.S., the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) <a href="https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2024/12/ftc-takes-action-against-gravy-analytics-venntel-unlawfully-selling-location-data-tracking-consumers">made</a> <a href="https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2024/12/ftc-takes-action-against-mobilewalla-collecting-selling-sensitive-location-data">clear</a> that their location data sales were unfair business practices in violation of federal law. <a href="https://yalelawandpolicy.org/end-running-warrants-purchasing-data-under-fourth-amendment-and-state-action-problem">Scholars</a>, <a href="https://www.wyden.senate.gov/news/press-releases/wyden-paul-and-bipartisan-senators-reintroduce-the-fourth-amendment-is-not-for-sale-act">lawmakers</a> and <a href="https://www.aclu.org/news/privacy-technology/dhs-is-circumventing-constitution-by-buying-data-it-would-normally-need-a-warrant-to-access">many</a> <a href="https://demandprogress.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/2026-03-19-Broad-coalition-opposes-FISA-reauth-until-AI-data-broker-loophole-is-closed.pdf">civil</a> <a href="https://epic.org/documents/join-comment-regarding-ombs-request-for-information-on-executive-branch-agency-handling-of-commercially-available-information">society</a> <a href="https://cdt.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/2021-12-08-Legal-Loopholes-and-Data-for-Dollars-Report-final.pdf">organizations</a> have considered the use of commercial data purchased from consumer data brokers and advertising firms for surveillance conducted by government agencies as a circumvention of the Fourth Amendment. In 2023, the DHS itself found in a <a href="https://www.oig.dhs.gov/sites/default/files/assets/2023-09/OIG-23-61-Sep23-Redacted.pdf">report</a> that its agencies violated federal law through their use of purchased location data, stating that ICE, CBP, and the Secret Service did not adhere to existing internal privacy policies and did not have sufficient policies and procedures in place.</p>



<p>In Europe and the U.K., the lawfulness of using the data is <a href="https://www.iccl.ie/rtb/">controversial</a> even for targeted advertising purposes. Consumer apps and digital advertising firms selling data to governments for surveillance purposes, and thus for entirely different purposes than what was stated to consumers, violates the principle of <a href="https://www.elgaronline.com/edcollchap/edcoll/9781800371675/9781800371675.00024.xml">purpose limitation</a>, a cornerstone of the European data protection regime. While the use of the data by governments for public safety and national security is subject to separate and different national legislation, its lawfulness is questionable and it lacks adequate oversight in <a href="https://www.interface-eu.org/publications/disproportionate-use-commercially-and-publicly-available-data-europes-next-frontier">several</a> <a href="https://www.ftm.nl/artikelen/toezicht-veiligheidsdiensten-osint">European</a> <a href="https://netzpolitik.org/2025/sicherheitsbehoerden-und-databroker-bundesregierung-macht-datenkauf-zum-staatsgeheimnis/">countries</a>.</p>



<h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Legal Justifications</strong></h3>



<p>In its <a href="https://citizenlab.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Citizen-Lab-Mail-Fwd_-Citizen-Lab-research-report_Redacted.pdf">response</a> to the Citizen Lab, Penlink says that it “obtains its location data from providers who obtain user consent for location data sharing through SDKs and who filter out sensitive locations from their datasets, consistent with FTC mandates.” Penlink did not answer our question about how it ensures that Webloc and its data sources do not violate privacy and data protection laws. Beyond Penlink’s response to this report, we are not aware of public statements that clearly explain how Penlink, and previously Cobwebs Technologies, obtain the data specifically used in the Webloc product in compliance with privacy and data protection legislation.</p>



<p>As discussed in <a href="#3-Webloc"><strong>Section 3</strong></a>, two documents that describe Webloc, dated 2021, claim that data collection complies with the GDPR and “various” privacy laws and emphasize that the data is collected with the “consent” of those who are monitored by the system. A promotional <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20220328214453/https://query.prod.cms.rt.microsoft.com/cms/api/am/binary/RWSzCB">brochure</a> from 2020 stated that Webloc provides the capability to “find anonymous threat actors.” The LAPD <a href="https://www.vice.com/en/article/the-lapd-is-using-controversial-mass-surveillance-tracking-software/">stated</a> that it uses “commercially available anonymized data,” when asked about Webloc.</p>



<p>Both the claims that data from mobile apps and digital advertising were “anonymized” and sold based on “consent” represent the two main <a href="https://virginialawreview.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/FriedmanCitron_Revised.pdf">legal justifications</a> used across the <a href="https://storage02.forbrukerradet.no/media/2020/01/2020-01-14-out-of-control-final-version.pdf">consumer data industry</a> and also by <a href="https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2022/08/inside-fog-data-science-secretive-company-selling-mass-surveillance-local-police">ad-based surveillance vendors</a>. </p>



<p>In Europe, under the GDPR, location records and behavioral data linked to Advertising IDs or other personal identifiers are not anonymous but <a href="https://swag.cispa.saarland/papers/nguyen2021gdpr.pdf">personal data</a>. The <a href="https://www.edpb.europa.eu/sites/default/files/files/file1/edpb_guidelines_202005_consent_en.pdf">high standard</a> that the GDPR sets for “informed” consent makes it unlikely that any actor in the supply chain, from mobile app vendors and advertising firms to ad-based surveillance vendors, can rely on valid consent for sharing data collected for the purpose of operating apps or digital advertising for surveillance purposes. </p>



<p>In the U.S., the FTC recently <a href="https://www.ftc.gov/system/files/ftc_gov/pdf/26AmendedComplaint%28unsealed%29.pdf">clarified</a> that Advertising IDs “offer no anonymity in the marketplace,” because “many” businesses “regularly link” those IDs “to other information about them, such as names, addresses, and phone numbers.” In a case against a data broker which relied on the “consent” of those whose location data was collected and sold to government agencies, the FTC <a href="https://www.ftc.gov/system/files/ftc_gov/pdf/212_3035_-_gravy_analytics_final_consent_package_without_signatures.pdf">determined</a> that consumers did not actually consent. We cannot verify Penlink’s claim in its <a href="https://citizenlab.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Citizen-Lab-Mail-Fwd_-Citizen-Lab-research-report_Redacted.pdf">response</a> to the Citizen Lab where it states that it obtains data from “providers who obtain consent.”</p>



<p>Even if location records would not include personal identifiers, such as an Advertising ID, they are not truly anonymous and can be re-identified, as academic research <a href="https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7961185/">has</a> <a href="https://netman.aiops.org/~peidan/ANM2016/Mobility/LectureCoverage/2011Mobicom_Anonymization%20of%20Location%20Data%20Does%20Not%20Work.pdf">often</a> <a href="https://www.osti.gov/pages/servlets/purl/1095747">shown</a>. As discussed in <a href="#3-Webloc"><strong>Section 3</strong></a>, identifying persons who use the tracked devices is, in fact, one of the purposes of Webloc.</p>



<p>Penlink recently <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/03/25/nx-s1-5752369/ice-surveillance-data-brokers-congress-anthropic">claimed</a> that Webloc’s data providers “filter out sensitive locations, such as hospitals, schools, and religious institutions,” reflecting one of several orders the FTC <a href="https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2024/12/ftc-takes-action-against-mobilewalla-collecting-selling-sensitive-location-data">recently</a> <a href="https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2024/12/ftc-takes-action-against-mobilewalla-collecting-selling-sensitive-location-data">imposed</a> on location data brokers. We do not know whether this claim is defensible. If it was, it addresses only one of several legal issues underlying Webloc’s data processing.</p>



<p>Penlink provides a generic <a href="https://www.penlink.com/privacy-policy/">privacy policy</a> on its website, which does not mention Webloc and covers everything from data processing on visitors of penlink.com to the collection of information from third-party sources and its disclosure to customers of Penlink’s “intelligence and analytics platforms”. It emphasizes that Penlink and its affiliates “value your privacy.” It explains that Penlink may receive data on individuals from “data brokers” and “other commercially available sources,” including name, email, phone number, and “historical information about the precise geolocation of your device,” and that it may disclose the information it collects with its customers. The policy also lists a number of “rights” people “may have” in the E.U., U.K., and several U.S. states, and links to a <a href="https://www.penlink.com/your-privacy-choices">page</a> where people can “opt out of sales of personal information to customers.” Penlink is registered as a “data broker” in the <a href="https://cppa.ca.gov/data_broker_registry/">California Data Broker Registry</a>.</p>



<h3 class="wp-block-heading" style="margin-bottom:var(--wp--preset--spacing--40)"><strong>Recommendations for States and Regulatory Bodies</strong></h3>



<ul class="wp-block-list">
<li>In Europe and the U.K., national data protection authorities are responsible for enforcing the GDPR, and in all but two E.U. member states also for enforcing the <a href="https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52022DC0364">Law Enforcement Directive (LED)</a>, which regulates personal data processing for law enforcement purposes. These authorities need to proactively investigate potential violations of the rights and freedoms of European data subjects due to the operation of Webloc and all entities involved in Webloc’s data supply chain.</li>



<li>Our findings suggest that European governments are particularly nontransparent about their potential use of ad-based surveillance technologies citing public safety and national security reasons. The public interest in a democratic debate about these technologies must be given higher priority than keeping information confidential for security reasons, specifically when it comes to law enforcement, and especially because the systems we examined enable highly intrusive mass surveillance.</li>



<li>Governments in Europe, U.K., U.S., and other regions must ensure that intrusive surveillance based on commercial data purchased from mobile apps, advertising firms and consumer data brokers does not infringe on civil liberties and fundamental rights by implementing adequate safeguards and democratic oversight.</li>



<li>Ad-based surveillance relies on the way <a href="https://storage02.forbrukerradet.no/media/2020/01/2020-01-14-out-of-control-final-version.pdf">mobile apps</a> and <a href="https://crackedlabs.org/en/rtb-security-crisis">digital advertising</a> currently operate, leading to uncontrolled data sharing with a large number of third parties. This broken digital infrastructure needs to be reformed at several levels, as <a href="https://tacd.org/consumer-and-digital-groups-in-europe-and-the-u-s-call-for-a-full-ban-on-surveillance-based-advertising/">consumer associations</a>, <a href="https://www.edpb.europa.eu/system/files/2021-11/edpb_statement_on_the_digital_services_package_and_data_strategy_en.pdf">regulators</a> and <a href="https://schakowsky.house.gov/media/press-releases/schakowsky-eshoo-wyden-booker-introduce-bill-ban-surveillance-advertising">policymakers</a> have long been demanding.</li>



<li>The urgent need to reform data practices in digital advertising and in the mobile app ecosystem is further aggravated by concerns about the broad availability of highly sensitive data on defense personnel and political leaders, which has been deemed a security risk by <a href="https://crackedlabs.org/en/rtb-security-crisis">civil society organizations</a> and <a href="https://www.nsa.gov/Press-Room/Press-Releases-Statements/Press-Release-View/Article/2298930/how-mobile-device-users-can-limit-their-location-data-exposure/">U.S. intelligence agencies</a> alike.</li>



<li>It is imperative that governments exercise rigorous due diligence regarding vendors when procuring surveillance technologies, including Webloc, Tangles, and other products. The assessment should include a detailed analysis of capabilities and data processing activities over the entire data supply chain in relation to legal requirements, potential abuses of the product, and the vendor’s broader business practices.</li>
</ul>



<h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Further Research </strong></h3>



<p>Based on our findings, we believe that further research would be fruitful with respect to:</p>



<ul class="wp-block-list">
<li>additional potential Webloc customers in Europe, in the U.K., U.S., and other regions where we received inconsistent or unsatisfactory responses to freedom of information requests, or found other indications for potential Webloc sales or usage,</li>



<li>Webloc’s data sources and data supply chain, i.e. app vendors, digital advertising firms or data brokers which the system obtains data from,</li>



<li>how Webloc is being used by law enforcement agencies and other customers and how this affects persons who are being tracked and profiled with the help of the system,</li>



<li>cases of mission creep, in which Webloc’s highly intrusive technology is used to investigate petty crimes, or cases falling outside of the appropriate scope of an agency’s mandate.</li>
</ul>



<p>This report is part of an ongoing series of investigations we are doing on the use of commercial data for surveillance purposes. We will be publishing subsequent investigations that explore areas for further research we have flagged in this report.</p>



<h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Protect Yourself from Ad-based Surveillance</strong></h3>



<p>Ad-based surveillance relies on data sent from the apps installed on your mobile device to third parties. Any app that displays advertisements is potentially affected. Apps that do not display ads may also directly or indirectly share user data with third parties. To minimize how apps installed on your device share data with third parties you can take the following steps:</p>



<ul class="wp-block-list">
<li>Apple iOS devices offer some protection against apps sharing data with third parties. When installing a new app, <a href="https://support.apple.com/en-us/102420">deny</a> it the permission to “track your activity across other companies’ apps and websites” during installation. <a href="https://support.apple.com/en-us/guide/iphone/iph4f4cbd242/ios">Review</a> the apps you have previously granted the permission to track you. This functionality is not available on Apple devices with an iOS version older than 14.5. In addition, <a href="https://support.apple.com/en-us/102515">review</a> the apps you may have granted the permission to access your location and other information from your device.</li>



<li>For Android devices, the “advertising ID” assigned to your device is key to any tracking and profiling carried out by third parties. Depending on the device vendor and Android version, <a href="https://privacy.ca.gov/tips/limit-mobile-device-tracking/">delete the advertising ID</a> or <a href="https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/6048248?hl=en">opt out of ads personalization</a> in the settings. In addition, <a href="https://privacy.ca.gov/tips/limit-mobile-device-tracking/">review</a> the apps you may have granted the permission to access your location and other information from your device.</li>
</ul>



<p>More information is available on the websites of the <a href="https://privacy.ca.gov/2025/09/limit-mobile-app-tracking/">California Privacy Protection Agency</a>, <a href="https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/protecting-your-information-and-data-when-using-applications-itsap40200">Canadian Centre for Cyber Security</a>, <a href="https://privacyinternational.org/guide-step/4339/ios-opt-out-targeted-ads-and-renew-your-ad-id">Privacy</a> <a href="https://privacyinternational.org/guide-step/4317/android-opt-out-targeted-ads-and-renew-your-advertising-id">International</a> and <a href="https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2022/05/how-disable-ad-id-tracking-ios-and-android-and-why-you-should-do-it-now">EFF</a>.</p>



<p>Following these recommendations, you can minimize but not reliably prevent apps from sharing data with third parties. A mobile app may still share data it processes for the purpose of operating the app on its servers directly with other companies. Google itself <a href="https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/6048248">states</a> that apps might use other “persistent or proprietary identifiers” when a user deletes the advertising ID on their device. <a href="https://proton.me/blog/meta-att-privacy-allegations">App vendors</a> and <a href="https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3531146.3533116">third parties</a> constantly try to find ways around existing protections.</p>
